COVID-19: How Africa kept pandemic at bay

By: Annalise Lubbe | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Tonight on Carte Blanche we look at Africa's seemingly remarkable escape from COVID-19 which has brought much of the world to its knees.

Unique Selling Point:
In April, as Covid-19 shut down country after country, the United Nations issued a stern warning: Africa might be next. Officials said Covid-19 could directly kill at least 300,00 people in Africa and possibly as many as 3.3. Million. In May, with infections and deaths still surprisingly low, the World Health Organisation revised that prediction down to between 83,000 and 190,000. There has been much speculation for Africa’s seemingly remarkable escape from a pandemic that has brought much of the world to its knees. To date, just over 40,000 Africans have lost their lives to Covid-19

Summary:
There is no single reason for Africa’s seemingly remarkable escape. For one, Africa consists of 54 countries that are ethnically and socially diverse. Yet, across the continent there are some trends that hint at why deaths form Covid-19 remain so low. The median age in Africa, where more than 60 percent of people are under the age of 25, is about half of that in Europe. This, combined with Africa’s warm climate and the potential of pre-existing immunity in some communities, has played a significant role. Thirdly, millions of citizens have developed a degree of immunity to Covid-19. Herd immunity defines the protection of a population from a virus through mild exposure to it. While South Africa may have unintendedly developed herd immunity against Covid-19, the World Health Organisation does not condone achieving herd immunity through public and unmonitored exposure to the virus. In South Africa’s case, the reported potential herd immunity was unintended. After easing lockdown restrictions in September, the country has managed to avoid a second wave of infections unlike other nations around the world.

Where countries in Europe are re-entering lockdown as a result of Covid-19 cases increasing, our local government has continued to report an unexpected drop in cases. Studies conducted in Western Cape and Gauteng have shown that up to 40% of people have developed coronavirus antibodies, with the majority unaware that they had ever been infected. The studies are ongoing to determine how much protection antibodies offer and for how long.


Further information:
Shabir Mahdi, a professor of vaccinology at the University of the Witwatersrand, said that he believes the coronavirus had generated a degree of immunity in approximately 12 to 15 million people in South Africa. “What has happened in SA today, the only plausible way to explain it is that some sort of herd immunity has been reached when combined with the use of non-pharmaceutical interventions...like the wearing of masks, physical distancing, ensuring ventilation when indoors, and so especially in heavily-populated townships that surround the major cities. Citizens were also expected to queue for essentials like food and social security grants during this period. Researchers believe that these measures created “new networks for the spread of the disease” and helped to fuel a huge wave of infections. “This inadequacy in terms of adherence of the lockdown, where inadvertently we’ve had transmission taking place, has resulted in a high percentage in densely populated areas becoming immune,” said Mahdi.

As some countries in Europe approach the cold winter months - creating the ideal condition for Covid-19 to survive longer in cooler temperatures, combined with people aggregating in closer numbers - record numbers of infection have been reported in the States and in the UK a second lock-down has been implemented. Africa’s overall warmer climate is therefore an advantage.

Thirdly, age plays a major role: with 60% of the African population being under 25 compared to Europe’s high percentage of people over 60, there are fewer Covid-19 deaths in Africa. “Understanding why children are only mildly affected” is part of a current study by Professor Heather Zar who is spearheading a funded research project to determine why children typically develop mild illness or have asymptomatic infection.” “In Africa, where children make up a large proportion of the population, prior infection with coronaviruses may have had an impact on the risk of infection”, she says.

One of the examples of an African country who has been widely praised for doing remarkably well with Covid-19 - considering there are only seven doctors for every 100, 000 people - was Senegal. With a population of around 16 million people, one third is living below the poverty line, and a vulnerable healthcare system, Senegal had to act swiftly when they were faced with their first case of Covid-19 in February from a Frenchman who returned to Dakar after a skiing holiday abroad.

A three-pronged strategy was devised to prevent and halt the level of community transmission quickly by isolating confirmed cases. This was done in the following way: deliver test results within 24 hours once samples were received by the laboratory; create a digital platform through which health workers was able to receive results from the surveillance teams; decentralise the districts by setting up a laboratory and sample collection in most regions possible to cut down on transportation delays. In terms of personal protective equipment supplies were sourced from major institutions and ongoing training ensured availability of skilled personnel.

To streamline the process further, a specialised laboratory was set up in Dakar to test for the disease. The laboratory, Institute Pasteur, was only one of two in Africa at the onset of the pandemic in February that was equipped to test for Covid-19. By April 43 countries on the African continent were able to diagnose Covid-19 effectively. Today the lab in Dakar has a 24-hour operation and testing has been expanded across the country. Tests for those with symptoms are free and results are released in 8 hours. While there have been concerns over low testing rates across the continent, there is hope that cheap self-testing diagnostic kits could help that effort.

The Institute Pastuer has been crucial to this effort, with its chief virologist Dr Amadou Sall in partnering with UK-based firm Mologic to develop two home test kits:
One - to test if someone currently has the virus, similarly to the currently used lab-based PCR swab tests; and two - to check if someone has developed antibodies for coronavirus from a previous infection. Dr. Sall says the manufacturing of the antibody test has already begun in a pilot study and will only cost $1 with results in just 10 minutes.

The lessons we learnt in Africa to keep the pandemic at bay have largely been to adhere to social distance and the use of non-pharmaceutical interventions. Mahdi points out that although we are positive in the fight against Covid-19 due to our experience with other coronaviruses, a mild infection is probably going to generate immunity for two or three years but that places us in a really good position but the response needs to be much more nuanced than simply believing that a highly restrictive lockdown is going to get rid of the virus,” he said.

Key interviews: Senegal - An interview with a representative of the Institut Pasteur: Dr. Amadou Sall to tell the success story of Senegal; an interview with Shjabir Mahdi - Prof of Vaccinology at the University of Witwatersrand to talk about the herd immunity in general and in South Africa; Prof Heather Zar - Director of the SA Medical Research Council and Chair of the Department of Paediatrics and Child Health to talk about the importance of the age group as mentioned earlier on and understanding why children are only mildly affected as well as infectious diseases and cross immunity which protects Africans from severe Covid-19.

Script:


Script: How Africa kept pandemic at bay
Duration: 8 Minutes
Date: 2 December 2020

LINK: in March COVID-19 shut down country after country. The United Nations issued a stern warning that the African continent could see as many as 300 000 deaths and possibly up to 3.3 million. But that didn’t happen.

Prof. Shabir Madhi: Head of Vaccinology: University of the Witwatersrand: What happened in Africa certainly is puzzling to many scientists and the predictions, including for myself was that Africa was going to be heavily affected.

V/O On the African continent, respiratory infections, like pneumonia, TB and HIV are some of the biggest risk factors and causes of death. Add COVID-19 to the list and it could spell disaster, is what everyone feared. Prof. Shabir Madhi, an expert in respiratory diseases, holds the theory that Africa’s youthful population played a role.

Prof Shabir Madhi: One of the narratives was the issue that Africa has a younger age group demographic. People over the age of 65 are 14 times more likely to die of covid-19 than those under the age of 65.

V/O In Europe the majority of the population is 60 and older - on the African continent, over half of the population is under 25.

Prof Heather Zar: Chair: Department of Paediatrics and Child Health: University of Cape Town: The global data is that children develop really mild illness, a very small minority require hospitalisation, and the number of children dying is fortunately teeny, teeny.

V/O Prof. Heather Zar has been working in Paarl, in the Western Cape for seven years to understand how coronavirus affects young children in the middle to low income groups. This year it’s been all about COVID-19 for the team.

Prof. Heather Zar: There are 4 coronaviruses that circulate all the time and generally they cause mild illness, a cold, and one of the theories is that children see these infections, develop antibodies to these mild coronaviruses and then are protected against covid and SARS-CoV-2.

V/O Whilst the youth may have been spared the worst, no-one knew whether public health systems on the continent would hold up in COVID-19 battle. A country like Senegal has only 7 doctors for every 100 000 people.

Dr Amadou Sall: Chief Virologist: Institut Pasteur, Dakar: People were worried because our health systems in general are weak and when we saw what happened in other countries with a much stronger system, people were worried that in Africa it may be terrible.

V/O Dr. Amadou Sall leads a team of specialists at the Institut Pasteur in Dakar, which has been helping 48 other countries with infectious diseases and training.

Macfarlane Moleli: Diseases like Ebola, HIV and Tuberculosis would you say that that made us a little bit more prepared to deal with something like the coronavirus?

Dr. Amadou Sall: Yes definitely, Ebola has been an amazing opportunity to train people and also build some capacity that was definitely useful.

V/O At the onset of the pandemic in February the Institut Pasteur was one of only two laboratories in Africa that could test for COVID - using a Rapid Diagnostic Testing kit to deliver test results in 24 hours.

Macfarlane Moleli: Your Rapid Diagnostic Testing kit, the PCR was this also made available for other African countries, especially those who did not have their own testing kits?

Dr. Amadou Sall: In cooperation with Africa CDC we distributed more than a million kits for the African region and sent them to more than 25 countries.

V/O In addition to Senegal’s top level testing and training that it exported to its neighbours, it was smart technology that made the difference in Rwanda - a country with among the lowest COVID-19 death rates on the continent. Rwanda deployed five human size robots to treatment centres in the capital Kigali. The robots perform temperature screening, vital signs readings, deliver video messages and even detect if people are wearing masks! One robot can screen 50 to 150 people a minute and report abnormalities. These smart machines played a key role in minimizing exposure from infected people to doctors and nurses working in high risk areas.

UP sound robot: “I have been so resourceful in countries like South Korea, Switzerland, Netherlands, Belgium and China, where the virus started and I look forward doing the same in Rwanda.”

V/O In Africa’s great cities, the fear was that close living quarters would fuel the spread of infection hotspots. Yet when many European countries and the United States saw wave after wave of runway infection, numbers on the African continent slowed down. For Madhi it’s explained by “herd immunity,” where people build up some protection or antibodies, so there is a break in transmission.

Prof. Shabir Madhi: For herd immunity to evolve against SARS-CoV-2 or COVID-19, you need to have at least 60 or 70% of the population that have developed immunity that will prevent them from passing on the virus to another person when they become exposed to the virus.

V/O But scientists warn about complacency - herd immunity cannot be a strategy to get on top of COVID-19, despite a relatively low mortality rate.

Prof. Shabir Madhi: The estimated infection mortality rate for South Africa is about one third of what it is for many other countries. In South Africa it is about 0.8 per 1000 whereas in other countries it is about 3 per 1000.

Prof. Heather Zar: One of the theories as to why low to middle income countries have not seen such a severe epidemic is that there is wide-spread vaccination with BCG and that that induces an immune response that is somewhat protective against COVID as well

V/O It now appears from medical research that Africa’s regular exposure to other coronaviruses, like the common cold, has helped build some resistance to COVID-19.

Prof. Shabir Madhi: What has been shown is that immunity against those common cold corona viruses in fact influences your immune response. And that itself might be actually protecting that infection progressing to severe disease.

V/O Sall’s team, supported by a British company, have designed a fast home-testing kit that’s already gone through pilot testing. At a cost of only $1 it shows in less than 10 minutes whether someone is positive. This proudly African innovation will be a game-changer when kits come off the assembly line in 2021.

Dr. Amadou Sall: That test actually started development in March.... from then until now we have been working on scaling up manufacturing and making it (according to) international standards... and we would be able to distribute early January and make it available to other countries.

V/O In Ghana, drone technology has allowed the government to monitor the spread of COVID-19 faster and reach more remote communities with medical supplies. The drones shuttle specimens for testing from suspected patients to the country's two biggest testing centres in Accra and Kumasi.

Up sound

V/O First health care workers place the order. Within an average of 30 minutes, deliveries are dispatched. The drones drop boxes of medical products by parachute at a designated spot. This emergency service has sped up diagnosis and helped the government track the pandemic by shortening the time between sample-taking and testing.

Up sound

V/O Whilst low mortality rates have been reported in Senegal, Ghana and Rwanda, Madhi warns that South Africa is not out of the woods yet. This country accounts for 51% of COVID-19 cases on the continent.

Prof. Shabir Madhi: To claim victory on African continent against COVID-19 pandemic right now is completely premature and it will result in citizens of the country of South Africa and elsewhere becoming complacent in terms of what needs to be done to prevent further deaths from COVID-19.

V/O. Getting ahead of the pandemic remains a complex challenge - but one that has revealed uniquely African values that have primed the continent for facing up to the task: like the names given to the robots: Urumuri, which means ‘light’, Ingabo - ‘shield’, and Ikizere - ‘hope’.

_______________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________

Promos
1.COVID-19 crippled the globe as infection rates soar again in the Northern Hemisphere. We ask why the pandemic seems to be presenting differently on the African continent.

2. We look at the African continent and reasons for being spared a second and third wave when many countries in Europe and the United States are facing a resurgence of COVID-19.

3. Smart technology, drones and robots, and a novel home-testing kit in development – we explore proudly African innovations that have helped in the fight against COVID-19.

Rwanda deployed five human size robots to treatment centres in the capital Kigali. The robots perform temperature screening, vital signs readings, deliver video messages and even detect if people are wearing masks! One robot can screen 50 to 150 people a minute and report abnormalities. These smart machines played a key role in minimizing exposure from infected people to doctors and nurses working in high risk areas. UP sound robot: “I have been so resourceful in countries like South Korea, Switzerland, Netherlands, Belgium and China, where the virus started and I look forward doing the same in Rwanda.” V/O In Africa’s great cities, the fear was that close living quarters would fuel the spread of infection hotspots. Yet when many European countries and the United States saw wave after wave of runway infection, numbers on the African continent slowed down. For Madhi it’s explained by “herd immunity,” where people build up some protection or antibodies, so there is a break in transmission. Prof. Shabir Madhi: For herd immunity to evolve against SARS-CoV-2 or COVID-19, you need to have at least 60 or 70% of the population that have developed immunity that will prevent them from passing on the virus to another person when they become exposed to the virus. V/O But scientists warn about complacency - herd immunity cannot be a strategy to get on top of COVID-19, despite a relatively low mortality rate. Prof. Shabir Madhi: The estimated infection mortality rate for South Africa is about one third of what it is for many other countries. In South Africa it is about 0.8 per 1000 whereas in other countries it is about 3 per 1000. Prof. Heather Zar: One of the theories as to why low to middle income countries have not seen such a severe epidemic is that there is wide-spread vaccination with BCG and that that induces an immune response that is somewhat protective against COVID as well V/O It now appears from medical research that Africa’s regular exposure to other coronaviruses, like the common cold, has helped build some resistance to COVID-19. Prof. Shabir Madhi: What has been shown is that immunity against those common cold corona viruses in fact influences your immune response. And that itself might be actually protecting that infection progressing to severe disease. V/O Sall’s team, supported by a British company, have designed a fast home-testing kit that’s already gone through pilot testing. At a cost of only $1 it shows in less than 10 minutes whether someone is positive. This proudly African innovation will be a game-changer when kits come off the assembly line in 2021. Dr. Amadou Sall: That test actually started development in March.... from then until now we have been working on scaling up manufacturing and making it (according to) international standards... and we would be able to distribute early January and make it available to other countries. V/O In Ghana, drone technology has allowed the government to monitor the spread of COVID-19 faster and reach more remote communities with medical supplies. The drones shuttle specimens for testing from suspected patients to the country's two biggest testing centres in Accra and Kumasi. Up sound V/O First health care workers place the order. Within an average of 30 minutes, deliveries are dispatched. The drones drop boxes of medical products by parachute at a designated spot. This emergency service has sped up diagnosis and helped the government track the pandemic by shortening the time between sample-taking and testing. Up sound V/O Whilst low mortality rates have been reported in Senegal, Ghana and Rwanda, Madhi warns that South Africa is not out of the woods yet. This country accounts for 51% of COVID-19 cases on the continent. Prof. Shabir Madhi: To claim victory on African continent against COVID-19 pandemic right now is completely premature and it will result in citizens of the country of South Africa and elsewhere becoming complacent in terms of what needs to be done to prevent further deaths from COVID-19. V/O. Getting ahead of the pandemic remains a complex challenge - but one that has revealed uniquely African values that have primed the continent for facing up to the task: like the names given to the robots: Urumuri, which means ‘light’, Ingabo - ‘shield’, and Ikizere - ‘hope’. _______________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________ Promos 1.COVID-19 crippled the globe as infection rates soar again in the Northern Hemisphere. We ask why the pandemic seems to be presenting differently on the African continent. 2. We look at the African continent and reasons for being spared a second and third wave when many countries in Europe and the United States are facing a resurgence of COVID-19. 3. Smart technology, drones and robots, and a novel home-testing kit in development – we explore proudly African innovations that have helped in the fight against COVID-19. _______________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________ Invoicing Back references from Insert ID in Invoice: Title Author Last Updated Invoice for COVID-19: How Africa kept pandemic at bay (5820) Annalise Lubbe 02 December 2020

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): Tonight on Carte Blanche we look at Africa's seemingly remarkable escape from COVID-19 which has brought much of the world to its knees.
metadata.Unique Selling Point: In April, as Covid-19 shut down country after country, the United Nations issued a stern warning: Africa might be next. Officials said Covid-19 could directly kill at least 300,00 people in Africa and possibly as many as 3.3. Million. In May, with infections and deaths still surprisingly low, the World Health Organisation revised that prediction down to between 83,000 and 190,000. There has been much speculation for Africa’s seemingly remarkable escape from a pandemic that has brought much of the world to its knees. To date, just over 40,000 Africans have lost their lives to Covid-19
metadata.Summary: There is no single reason for Africa’s seemingly remarkable escape. For one, Africa consists of 54 countries that are ethnically and socially diverse. Yet, across the continent there are some trends that hint at why deaths form Covid-19 remain so low. The median age in Africa, where more than 60 percent of people are under the age of 25, is about half of that in Europe. This, combined with Africa’s warm climate and the potential of pre-existing immunity in some communities, has played a significant role. Thirdly, millions of citizens have developed a degree of immunity to Covid-19. Herd immunity defines the protection of a population from a virus through mild exposure to it. While South Africa may have unintendedly developed herd immunity against Covid-19, the World Health Organisation does not condone achieving herd immunity through public and unmonitored exposure to the virus. In South Africa’s case, the reported potential herd immunity was unintended. After easing lockdown restrictions in September, the country has managed to avoid a second wave of infections unlike other nations around the world. Where countries in Europe are re-entering lockdown as a result of Covid-19 cases increasing, our local government has continued to report an unexpected drop in cases. Studies conducted in Western Cape and Gauteng have shown that up to 40% of people have developed coronavirus antibodies, with the majority unaware that they had ever been infected. The studies are ongoing to determine how much protection antibodies offer and for how long.
metadata.Further information: Shabir Mahdi, a professor of vaccinology at the University of the Witwatersrand, said that he believes the coronavirus had generated a degree of immunity in approximately 12 to 15 million people in South Africa. “What has happened in SA today, the only plausible way to explain it is that some sort of herd immunity has been reached when combined with the use of non-pharmaceutical interventions...like the wearing of masks, physical distancing, ensuring ventilation when indoors, and so especially in heavily-populated townships that surround the major cities. Citizens were also expected to queue for essentials like food and social security grants during this period. Researchers believe that these measures created “new networks for the spread of the disease” and helped to fuel a huge wave of infections. “This inadequacy in terms of adherence of the lockdown, where inadvertently we’ve had transmission taking place, has resulted in a high percentage in densely populated areas becoming immune,” said Mahdi. As some countries in Europe approach the cold winter months - creating the ideal condition for Covid-19 to survive longer in cooler temperatures, combined with people aggregating in closer numbers - record numbers of infection have been reported in the States and in the UK a second lock-down has been implemented. Africa’s overall warmer climate is therefore an advantage. Thirdly, age plays a major role: with 60% of the African population being under 25 compared to Europe’s high percentage of people over 60, there are fewer Covid-19 deaths in Africa. “Understanding why children are only mildly affected” is part of a current study by Professor Heather Zar who is spearheading a funded research project to determine why children typically develop mild illness or have asymptomatic infection.” “In Africa, where children make up a large proportion of the population, prior infection with coronaviruses may have had an impact on the risk of infection”, she says. One of the examples of an African country who has been widely praised for doing remarkably well with Covid-19 - considering there are only seven doctors for every 100, 000 people - was Senegal. With a population of around 16 million people, one third is living below the poverty line, and a vulnerable healthcare system, Senegal had to act swiftly when they were faced with their first case of Covid-19 in February from a Frenchman who returned to Dakar after a skiing holiday abroad. A three-pronged strategy was devised to prevent and halt the level of community transmission quickly by isolating confirmed cases. This was done in the following way: deliver test results within 24 hours once samples were received by the laboratory; create a digital platform through which health workers was able to receive results from the surveillance teams; decentralise the districts by setting up a laboratory and sample collection in most regions possible to cut down on transportation delays. In terms of personal protective equipment supplies were sourced from major institutions and ongoing training ensured availability of skilled personnel. To streamline the process further, a specialised laboratory was set up in Dakar to test for the disease. The laboratory, Institute Pasteur, was only one of two in Africa at the onset of the pandemic in February that was equipped to test for Covid-19. By April 43 countries on the African continent were able to diagnose Covid-19 effectively. Today the lab in Dakar has a 24-hour operation and testing has been expanded across the country. Tests for those with symptoms are free and results are released in 8 hours. While there have been concerns over low testing rates across the continent, there is hope that cheap self-testing diagnostic kits could help that effort. The Institute Pastuer has been crucial to this effort, with its chief virologist Dr Amadou Sall in partnering with UK-based firm Mologic to develop two home test kits: One - to test if someone currently has the virus, similarly to the currently used lab-based PCR swab tests; and two - to check if someone has developed antibodies for coronavirus from a previous infection. Dr. Sall says the manufacturing of the antibody test has already begun in a pilot study and will only cost $1 with results in just 10 minutes. The lessons we learnt in Africa to keep the pandemic at bay have largely been to adhere to social distance and the use of non-pharmaceutical interventions. Mahdi points out that although we are positive in the fight against Covid-19 due to our experience with other coronaviruses, a mild infection is probably going to generate immunity for two or three years but that places us in a really good position but the response needs to be much more nuanced than simply believing that a highly restrictive lockdown is going to get rid of the virus,” he said. Key interviews: Senegal - An interview with a representative of the Institut Pasteur: Dr. Amadou Sall to tell the success story of Senegal; an interview with Shjabir Mahdi - Prof of Vaccinology at the University of Witwatersrand to talk about the herd immunity in general and in South Africa; Prof Heather Zar - Director of the SA Medical Research Council and Chair of the Department of Paediatrics and Child Health to talk about the importance of the age group as mentioned earlier on and understanding why children are only mildly affected as well as infectious diseases and cross immunity which protects Africans from severe Covid-19. ___________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________
